parts.name: Foundations
parts.blurb: This is the bedrock — the why and who underneath everything else. Get these right and every design choice later gets easier, because you'll know what you're expressing. Take your time here.

sections.title: Brand Story
sections.tag: The reason your brand exists — and the world it's trying to build.
sections.desc: Your brand story isn't a résumé or a timeline. It's the why underneath everything: where the brand came from, what it refuses to accept, and the future it's working toward. Told well, it makes a stranger feel like they already understand you. Keep it human. Write the way you'd tell a friend on a walk — plain, honest, specific. A little tension helps (something you're pushing against), because that's what makes people care.
sections.ex: "Fernloom started at a kitchen table, pouring candles for friends who couldn't find any that felt honest — everything on the shelf was mass-made and smelled like a chemistry set. We refuse the throwaway version of comfort, so we make small-batch candles and ceramics, by hand, meant to be kept. We're building a home-goods brand for people who want their everyday rituals to feel like a little ceremony."
sections.intro: Let's build this together, one small step at a time. Don't try to write it perfectly yet — just answer each step honestly. We'll stitch it into a story at the end. Bullet points are completely fine.

fields.label: Where did it begin?
fields.hint: The moment, place, or feeling that started it. Just a few words.

fields.label: What frustrated you — or what do you refuse to accept?
fields.hint: What felt broken or missing that you wanted to fix?

fields.label: Who is this really for?
fields.hint: Picture one real person who needs what you make.

fields.label: What future are you building toward?
fields.hint: If this works, what changes for them?

fields.label: Now bring it together.
fields.hint: Write it as 3–4 sentences: start with the beginning, add the spark, name your people, end on the future. You've already done the hard part.

sections.title: Founder Story
sections.tag: The human behind the brand — because people trust people.
sections.desc: Even a product or an app has a person or a moment behind it. Your founder story is the honest arc: where you started, the turn that changed things, what it cost you, and what you carry into the work now. It doesn't need to be dramatic — it needs to be true. This is often what makes someone choose you over a bigger, shinier option. They're not just buying the thing; they're buying who made it.
sections.ex: "Our founder was a nurse for nine years. Burned out and looking for something slower, she started making candles at night — a craft with her hands instead of a screen. What began as a way to breathe became a brand. She brings the same thing to every order she brought to nursing: care you can feel."
sections.intro: No need to write a memoir. Four honest lines will do it. Answer each, then we'll shape it.

fields.label: Where did you start — before this brand?
fields.hint: Your background, your "before." One or two lines.

fields.label: What was the turning point?
fields.hint: The moment you decided to make this. What shifted?

fields.label: What did it take? (optional, but powerful)
fields.hint: A cost, a risk, a leap. Honesty builds trust.

fields.label: What do you carry into the work now?
fields.hint: The value or skill from your "before" that still shows up.

fields.label: Bring it together.
fields.hint: Three or four sentences, first person. Start with the before, name the turn, land on what you bring now.

sections.title: Core Values
sections.tag: The tie-breakers you reach for when a decision is hard.
sections.desc: Values aren't wall art. They're the handful of principles you'd actually defend under pressure — the ones that decide a close call. If a value doesn't change a decision, it isn't really a value; it's a nice word. Aim for three to seven. Each one should come with a behavior, so it's a thing you do, not just a thing you say.
sections.ex: Craft — made by hand, or not at all. Calm — every touchpoint should slow you down, not speed you up. Honesty — real ingredients, real story, no filler. Sustainability — reusable vessels, low-waste shipping. Warmth — treat every customer like a guest.
sections.intro: We'll find your values by starting wide and narrowing down . Don't judge your first ideas — just get them out.

fields.label: Brain-dump 10–15 words you admire.
fields.hint: What do you respect in people, brands, or work? Don't overthink.

fields.label: Circle the 3–7 you'd defend even when it costs you.
fields.hint: Which ones would you keep on a bad day?

fields.label: For each keeper, name the behavior it demands.
fields.hint: Finish: "This means we always ___ / never ___."

fields.label: Gut-check.
fields.hint: Would you hire, fire, or say no to money over this value? If yes, it's real.

sections.title: Mission
sections.tag: What you do, for whom, and how — in one honest sentence.
sections.desc: Your mission is a present-tense sentence: what you do, who you do it for, and the way only you do it. Say it out loud — if it could belong to any brand in your space, it isn't sharp enough yet. It's a compass, not a slogan. When you're unsure whether to take a project or add a feature, the mission answers "is this us?"
sections.ex: "We make small-batch candles and ceramics that turn everyday rituals into moments of calm — for people who want their home to feel like a sanctuary."
sections.intro: We'll build your mission from three simple pieces , then snap them together.

fields.label: What do you actually do?
fields.hint: The plain verb + thing. "We make…," "We help…," "We teach…"

fields.label: Who is it for?
fields.hint: Be specific — a real kind of person, not "everyone."

fields.label: What's your unique how?
fields.hint: The approach or feeling only you bring to it.

fields.label: Snap it together.
fields.hint: "We exist to ___ (do what), for ___ (whom), by ___ (your unique how)." Then smooth it into one clean sentence.

sections.title: Vision
sections.tag: The bigger world you're walking toward.
sections.desc: If your mission is what you do now, your vision is the world you're moving toward — the horizon you're walking to even if you never fully arrive. It should feel a little bigger than you, and a little inspiring to say. You only need one or two sentences. It's the north star everything else points at.
sections.ex: "A world where people slow down on purpose — where the objects in a home are made by someone who cared, and rest isn't a luxury but a daily habit."
sections.intro: Let yourself dream a little here. There are no wrong answers — just picture it.

fields.label: Imagine it's ten years out and you've succeeded. What's different in the world?
fields.hint: For your people, your industry, or your corner of it.

fields.label: Finish this: "We're building toward a world where…"
fields.hint: One or two sentences. Big is okay here.

sections.title: Tagline & Slogans
sections.tag: The lines that stick — said for the ear, not the page.
sections.desc: A tagline is the one line that travels with your name. Slogans flex by campaign or season. Mantras are the things you say to yourselves to stay on track. Write all of them for the ear — if it sounds good said out loud, it'll spread. Shorter is almost always stronger. Aim for something a stranger could remember after hearing it once.
sections.ex: Tagline: "Light something good." · Seasonal slogan: "Made slow, kept long." · Internal mantra: "If we wouldn't keep it, we don't sell it."
sections.intro: We'll collect raw phrases first, then polish . Ugly first drafts are welcome — that's how good lines are found.

fields.label: Jot 5–10 phrases you already say about what you do.
fields.hint: How you'd describe it to a friend. Steal from your own mouth.

fields.label: Circle the promise underneath them.
fields.hint: What's the one feeling or result you keep pointing at?

fields.label: Write your tagline in 7 words or fewer.
fields.hint: Say each version out loud. Cut a word. Say it again.

fields.label: Add two slogans and one internal mantra.
fields.hint: Slogans face the world; the mantra faces you.

sections.title: Brand Niche
sections.tag: The specific corner you own — and no one owns quite like you.
sections.desc: Your niche is the narrow-but-meaningful corner you own: who you're for, what you do, and the twist that's yours. It can feel scary to narrow down — but "for everyone" reaches no one. The riches really are in the niches. Narrowing doesn't shrink you; it makes you findable and memorable. You can always grow outward from a strong center.
sections.ex: "Hand-poured candles paired with keepable, handmade ceramic vessels — for people making their homes calmer, who'd rather own one beautiful thing than five disposable ones."
sections.intro: We'll build your niche from three answers , then write one clean sentence. Specific beats broad every time.

fields.label: Who exactly is it for?
fields.hint: Narrow it. "Busy new parents," not "families." "Solo founders," not "businesses."

fields.label: What do you do for them?
fields.hint: The core thing they get.

fields.label: What's the twist only you bring?
fields.hint: The angle, method, or feeling that's distinctly yours.

fields.label: Write it as one sentence.
fields.hint: "We help ___ (who) do ___ (what) by ___ (your twist) — unlike ___ (the usual option)."

parts.name: Brand Personality
parts.blurb: If Part One was the why , this is the who — how your brand shows up in a room. How it sounds, how it feels, who it's for, and the character people come to recognize. This is where your brand starts to feel like a person.

sections.title: Positioning & USP
sections.tag: The sentence that lives in your customer's head — and the thing only you can claim.
sections.desc: Positioning is the space you own in someone's mind: the category you're in and why you win it. Your USP (unique selling proposition) is the "only" statement — the honest claim a competitor can't copy. You're not trying to be everything. You're trying to be the obvious choice for a specific person with a specific need.
sections.ex:
Position: "The candle you keep the jar from."
USP: "The only small-batch candle maker that pairs each scent with a matching handmade ceramic vessel you'll reuse long after the candle's gone."
sections.intro: We'll find your position by naming the alternative and then stepping away from it.

fields.label: What category are you in — in plain words?
fields.hint: "A candle brand." "A budgeting app." "A wedding photographer."

fields.label: What's the usual option people choose instead — and what's wrong with it?
fields.hint: Name the competitor or the status quo, and the gap it leaves.

fields.label: Finish: "We're the only ___ that ___."
fields.hint: Your honest "only." If it's not quite true yet, make it true.

fields.label: Now write your one-line position.
fields.hint: Short enough to say in one breath.

sections.title: Your People (Audience)
sections.tag: One real person you're building for — not "everyone."
sections.desc: The clearest brands picture one real person and speak straight to them. When you try to talk to everyone, you sound like no one. Build a persona: who they are, what keeps them up at night, and what they secretly want. You can have more than one — but start with the one who needs you most.
sections.ex: "Maya, 34. Works a lot, nests hard on weekends. Loves her space but hates clutter and cheap stuff that breaks. Secretly wants her home to feel like an exhale. Finds us on Instagram and in slow-living newsletters."
sections.intro: Picture one specific person and introduce them to us. Give them a name — it makes them real.

fields.label: Name & quick sketch.
fields.hint: Name, age-ish, what their days look like.

fields.label: What's their pain — the thing they're frustrated by?
fields.hint: The problem you quietly solve.

fields.label: What do they secretly want?
fields.hint: The deeper wish under the practical need.

fields.label: Where do they hang out — and how do they find you?
fields.hint: Platforms, places, people they trust.

sections.title: Brand Essence
sections.tag: Your whole brand, in one breath.
sections.desc: Essence is the feeling underneath everything — three to seven words, or one tight line, that capture the soul of the brand. It's not a slogan you publish; it's the tuning fork you check everything against.
sections.ex: "Calm you can hold."
sections.intro: We'll get there by going small , not big. Fewer words, more truth.

fields.label: Three words that feel like your brand.
fields.hint: Not features — feelings. Warm? Sharp? Wild? Steady?

fields.label: Now squeeze it into one short phrase.
fields.hint: Three to five words. Say it until it feels right.

sections.title: Personality Traits
sections.tag: If your brand walked into a room, how would it carry itself?
sections.desc: Pick four to six human traits and hold them steadily. Personality is what makes people feel like they know you — and it's a filter for everything from your captions to your customer emails. It helps to also name what you're not, so the edges stay crisp.
sections.ex: Warm · Unhurried · Honest · Grounded · Quietly witty. Not: loud, trendy, or precious. In one line: "the calm friend with good taste who never rushes you."
sections.intro: Choose your handful, then guard the edges with a "not" list.

fields.label: Pick 4–6 traits your brand carries.
fields.hint: Human words. Imagine describing a person, not a company.

fields.label: Name 2–3 things you're NOT.
fields.hint: The nearby traits you want to avoid.

fields.label: Sum it up in one line.
fields.hint: "The ___ friend who ___."

sections.title: Brand Vibe
sections.tag: The mood people feel in your world before they read a word.
sections.desc: Vibe is atmosphere. Capture it with keywords and a scene — a little world someone could step into. It's what guides your colors, music, imagery, and pace later on.
sections.ex: Keywords: warm, earthy, calm, tactile, honest, soft. The scene: "a sunlit studio that smells like citrus and wet clay, a kettle going, hands shaping a bowl, no rush anywhere in the room."
sections.intro: Paint us a little picture. Sensory beats abstract — what would we see, hear, smell?

fields.label: Six vibe keywords.
fields.hint: Adjectives that set the mood.

fields.label: Describe the scene of your world in a sentence or two.
fields.hint: If your brand were a place, what's it like to stand there?

fields.label: Two "not this, but this" reframes.
fields.hint: e.g., "not corporate — warm and human."

sections.title: Brand Archetype
sections.tag: The recognizable role your brand plays.
sections.desc: Archetypes are timeless characters that make a brand instantly legible — the Sage (wisdom), the Rebel (change), the Creator (imagination), the Caregiver (nurture), the Ruler (excellence), the Explorer (freedom), the Hero (courage), the Everyperson (belonging), the Lover (intimacy), the Jester (joy), the Innocent (simplicity), the Magician (transformation). Pick one primary. You can add a supporting one for nuance, but a clear lead keeps you legible.
sections.ex: Primary: The Caregiver — nurturing, warm, makes you feel looked-after. Supporting: The Creator — pride in the craft and the hands behind it.
sections.intro: Pick from the list above. Trust your gut — the first one you're drawn to is usually right.

fields.label: My primary archetype is…
fields.hint: The one role that fits best.

fields.label: Why? How does it show up in what you do?
fields.hint: One or two examples.

fields.label: A supporting archetype (optional) and its role.
fields.hint: The flavor it adds.

sections.title: Brand Culture
sections.tag: How your brand behaves when no one's performing.
sections.desc: Culture is how you work, how you treat people, and how you mark moments. Even a solo brand has a culture — the standards and rhythms baked into how it operates. Naming it keeps you consistent as you grow.
sections.ex: "Slow mornings, hands busy, music on. We make it by hand or we don't make it. We'd rather ship ten things we're proud of than a hundred we're not." Ritual: the first pour of every new scent gets lit and shared with the team before it goes on sale.
sections.intro: Three honest answers. Describe how it really is (or how you want it to be).

fields.label: How do you work? (your norms)
fields.hint: Pace, standards, how decisions get made.

fields.label: How do you treat people — customers and collaborators?
fields.hint: The felt experience of dealing with you.

fields.label: One ritual or tradition that marks a moment.
fields.hint: A launch ritual, a thank-you habit, a milestone you celebrate.

sections.title: Brand Promise
sections.tag: The thing people can count on, every single time.
sections.desc: Your promise is what stays true on your best day and your worst. Keep it specific and keepable — a modest promise you always hit builds more trust than a big one you break.
sections.ex: "Every piece is made by hand, made to last, and made to order — and if it arrives less than perfect, we remake it, no questions."
sections.intro: Promise only what you can keep on a bad week . That's what makes it real.

fields.label: What can people always count on from you?
fields.hint: The one standard you never drop.

fields.label: Write it as a promise, out loud.
fields.hint: Start with "You can always count on us to…" then tighten.

sections.title: Brand Themes
sections.tag: The handful of ideas your brand keeps circling back to.
sections.desc: Themes are your recurring notes — the topics and ideas everything you make reinforces. Name a few and your content, products, and story all start pulling in the same direction.
sections.ex: Slow living · Everyday ritual · Handmade craft · Keep, don't toss. Unifying line: "Make the ordinary feel like a ceremony."
sections.intro: Find the threads you already keep pulling on .

fields.label: List the ideas you keep coming back to.
fields.hint: In your posts, your products, your conversations.

fields.label: Circle your 3–5 core themes.
fields.hint: The ones most central to you.

fields.label: Write one line that ties them together.
fields.hint: Your north-star sentence.

sections.title: Experience & Emotions
sections.tag: How it feels to move through your brand — and what people walk away with.
sections.desc: Two things to name: the emotion you want at each stage of the journey, and the split between how people feel (emotional) and what they get (functional). The best brands nail both — the feeling pulls people in, the function keeps them.
sections.ex: Journey: Discovery (curious, calmed) → Buying (reassured) → Unboxing (delighted, "this was made for me") → After (loyal). Feel: calm, cared for, a little spoiled. Get: clean-burning candles, reusable vessels, honest labels, low-waste packaging.
sections.intro: Walk your customer's path and name the feeling at each stop .

fields.label: Feeling at each stage: discovery → first contact → during → after.
fields.hint: One word per stage is plenty.

fields.label: How do you want people to FEEL?
fields.hint: The emotional payoff.

fields.label: What do you want them to GET?
fields.hint: The practical, functional value.

sections.title: Brand Motivation
sections.tag: The deeper "why" that keeps you going when it's hard.
sections.desc: Beyond the product, what belief is your brand really in service of? Your motivation is the fuel — the thing that makes the hard days worth it and gives your work meaning past the sale.
sections.ex: "Because rest isn't a reward you earn — it's a right. If a candle and a quiet ten minutes help someone remember that, the work matters."
sections.intro: Go one layer deeper than "to make money." What do you really believe?

fields.label: What keeps you going, underneath it all?
fields.hint: Finish: "Because…"

fields.label: How will you measure success beyond money?
fields.hint: "We measure success by ___."

parts.name: Voice, Tone & Language
parts.blurb: Everything you say — and everywhere you say it — is your brand. This is the deepest part of the book on purpose: from the big voice down to a single button, from the feelings you engineer to the way you handle a hard conversation. Work the sections that fit you and skip the ones that don't — they'll be here the day you need them.

sections.title: Your Brand Voice
sections.tag: Your personality in words — the part that never changes.
sections.desc: Voice is who you are in language, constant everywhere you write. The cleanest way to lock it is a contrast: "We are ___, not ___." Naming what you're not keeps the edges sharp. And a rule worth keeping: never name a voice trait without a sample sentence that proves it.
sections.ex: Warm, not gushy · Plain-spoken, not corporate · Quietly witty, not goofy. Voice line: "We sound like a maker talking to you across a table."
sections.intro: Three attributes, each with a guardrail and a sample line.

fields.label: Pick 3 words for how your brand sounds.
Write your one-line voice statement + one sample sentence.

sections.title: Founder / Spokesperson Voice
sections.tag: The human layer living inside the brand voice.
sections.desc: Behind most brand voices is one real person whose natural way of talking is the brand's warmth. Capturing that personal fingerprint — your baseline energy and your signature way of explaining things — keeps the voice from ever going generic, and makes it easy to hand off (a teammate or a tool can write "as you").
sections.ex: The founder writes like she's handing you a warm mug — unhurried, plain, a little wry. Her signature move: explain with a small everyday comparison first, then the how. ("A candle's like bread — the first bake sets the loaf.")
sections.intro: Capture the person behind the brand in three strokes.

fields.label: Your baseline energy, as a metaphor.
fields.hint: "Like a walk in the park." "Like a calm mug of tea." "Like a hype coach."

fields.label: Your signature way of explaining things.
fields.hint: Analogy first? Story first? Straight to the steps?

sections.title: Tone — Reading the Room
sections.tag: Same voice, different moments.
sections.desc: Voice never changes; tone flexes for the moment. You'd celebrate a win differently than you'd deliver hard news. Match the reader's emotional state first, then guide them where you want to go.
sections.exWho: Fernloom Goods — one voice, three tones
sections.ex: Launch: "It's here — and it smells like a Sunday morning." Apology: "Your order's a few days behind, and that's on us." Teaching: "First burn matters most — let it melt to the edge."
sections.intro: Practice your voice in three real emotional moments.

fields.label: Something went wrong — an honest, kind line.

sections.title: Voice Spectrum & Calibration
sections.tag: Your voice as dials you can turn up or down.
sections.desc: Think of your voice as a few sliders, each 1–5. You have a default setting — but you nudge the dials for the moment (more formal for a policy, more playful for a launch). Naming the sliders makes tone a decision instead of a guess.
sections.ex: Casual 1—2—3—4—5 Formal · Playful 1—2—3—4—5 Serious · Warm 1—2—3—4—5 Cool. "Light something good" (default) → "We're pleased to introduce our new collection" (dialed formal).
sections.intro: Build your dials, set your default, then calibrate.

fields.label: Name 3 sliders and mark your default (1–5).
fields.hint: e.g., Casual↔Formal, Playful↔Serious, Warm↔Cool.

fields.label: Where do the dials move for a formal moment vs a casual one?
Write one sentence at two different settings.

sections.title: Your Voice & Tone Matrix
sections.tag: A quick-reference so anyone writing for you gets it right.
sections.desc: A matrix is a cheat-sheet: for each place you show up, the tone to use and a quick do/don't. It's what keeps you consistent when you're busy or handing writing to someone else.
sections.ex: Website: warm — do lead with feeling, don't oversell. Support: calm — do reassure, don't jargon. Social: playful — do sound human, don't be salesy. Bad news: honest — do own it fast.
sections.intro: Fill this for the four places you show up most: tone word + a do & a don't.

sections.title: Psychological Design Language
sections.tag: The beliefs your experience quietly acts on.
sections.desc: Underneath the words and the look, your brand takes a stance toward the person: it assumes something about them and reinforces a belief with every interaction. Do you assume they're capable, or that they need hand-holding? Is a purchase a transaction, or a small ceremony? Naming this makes your whole experience intentional instead of accidental.
sections.ex: Assumes: you deserve calm and you have good taste. So a product page feels like a slow browse, not a hard sell; an unboxing is treated like a small ritual, not a shipment. The quiet message: "you're the kind of person who keeps beautiful things."
sections.intro: Name the stance your brand takes toward your person.

fields.label: What do you assume about your person?
fields.hint: Capable? Overwhelmed? Curious? Skeptical? In a hurry?

fields.label: What belief should each interaction quietly reinforce?
fields.hint: "You're safe here." "You've got this." "You belong."

fields.label: Finish one reframe: "We treat ___ like ___."
fields.hint: "We treat checkout like a handshake, not a form."

sections.title: Emotional Design Language
sections.tag: The exact feelings you engineer — on purpose.
sections.desc: Separate from how you look or sound, name the specific emotions your brand is built to produce. Most brands leave this to chance; strong ones choose a small palette of feelings and design every touchpoint to deliver them. Feelings are the thing people actually remember.
sections.ex: Calm · Cared-for · A little spoiled · Unhurried · Quietly proud. Mapped: Discovery → curious calm · Buying → reassured · Unboxing → "this was made for me."
sections.intro: Choose your feelings, then place them where they happen.

fields.label: List 5–7 emotions your brand is engineered to create.
Map one feeling to each key moment (discovery / buying / after).
The one feeling above all others.

sections.title: Key Messages & Hierarchy
sections.tag: The handful of things you want remembered — in order.
sections.desc: Your key messages are the two or three ideas you want to land every time. Lead with the most important — people rarely read to the end. Pair them with a tight one-liner and a two-sentence elevator pitch.
sections.ex: One-liner: "Hand-poured candles in ceramics worth keeping." Messages: made by hand · the vessel is yours to keep · honest ingredients.
sections.intro: Small to big: one-liner, three messages, a pitch.

fields.label: Your top 3 messages, most important first, each with a proof point.

sections.title: Message Skeleton & Draft Template
sections.tag: A repeatable shape so anything you write lands on-brand.
sections.desc: Beyond what you say, give yourself a shape to say it in — a few beats every message follows. Turn it into a fill-in-the-blank template and drafting an email, a post, or a pitch stops being a blank-page fight.
sections.ex: Connect (a human hello) → Context (why this, why now) → Offer (the thing + one benefit) → Warm close (a gentle next step). Template: "Hey [name] — [seasonal hello]. We just [what]. It [benefit]. [Soft CTA]."
sections.intro: Build your beats, then make them a fill-in template.

fields.label: Turn them into a fill-in-the-blank template.
Draft one real message using it.

sections.title: Words You Use, Words You Avoid
sections.tag: Your brand's own little dictionary.
sections.desc: Brands have signature words — and forbidden ones. Naming both keeps your language recognizable and makes handoffs safe. Include a jargon rule: whether you use industry terms and how you keep them plain.
sections.ex: Love: small-batch, kept, ritual, by hand. Avoid: luxury, cheap, disrupt, "grab yours now." Jargon rule: explain any craft term in the same breath.
sections.intro: Start your lists — even five each helps.

sections.title: Signature Phrases & Verbal Tics
sections.tag: The lines that are yours — and the habits to watch.
sections.desc: A step past your word lists: your signature phrases (the lines you repeat on purpose, and why each earns its place) and your verbal tics — the habits that sneak in and soften you (over-apologizing, hedging, filler). Naming a tic is how you catch it.
sections.ex: Signature: "Made slow, kept long" (the whole promise in four words). Tic to watch: over-apologizing — swap "so sorry for the wait" → "thanks for your patience."
sections.intro: Catalog your best lines, then flag a habit to manage.

fields.label: A verbal tic you overuse.
fields.hint: Over-apologizing? "Just"? "I think"? Exclamation points?

fields.label: Its antidote — what you'll write instead.

sections.title: Grammar, Style & Mechanics
sections.tag: The small, consistent choices that make you look put-together.
sections.desc: You don't need to be a grammar expert — you need to pick a house style once and stick to it. A useful frame: choose a base style guide (like AP), then list your intentional exceptions.
sections.ex: Base: AP, with exceptions. Contractions: yes. Sentences: short. Oxford comma: yes. Headlines: sentence case. Numbers: spell out one–nine. Emoji: rarely, never in support.
sections.intro: Make your house-style calls — no wrong answers, just pick.

fields.label: Base style guide + your top exceptions.
Contractions? Sentence length? Oxford comma? Capitalization? Numbers?
Emoji & exclamation points — when, if ever?

sections.title: Naming & Nomenclature
sections.tag: How you name the things you make.
sections.desc: How you name products, tiers, and features is part of your voice. Pick a theme or rule and your names start doing marketing for you — instead of leaning on "Pro," "Plus," and "Premium." Keep a small glossary so everyone uses terms the same way.
sections.ex: Scents named after times of day: Morning Clay, Midday Citrus, Last Light. Glossary keeps "cure time," "cold throw," and "vessel" defined once.
sections.intro: Find a naming theme, then test it.

fields.label: Name three real things with it.
Two brand terms to define in your glossary.

sections.title: Writing for Every Surface
sections.tag: The same voice, shaped for the job each word has to do.
sections.desc: A headline, a button, an error, and an email each have a different job — but all sound like you. Master this and your brand feels whole everywhere. Website Lead with the benefit; headlines a skimmer gets in two seconds; buttons that say what happens next ("Find your scent," not "Submit"). App / product microcopy Clear over clever; verbs on buttons; empty states tell people what to do first; errors never blame the user — say what happened and how to fix it. Social & email Social: sound like a person, give value before you ask. Email: honest subject lines, greet like a human, one idea per email, sign off in your voice.
sections.ex: Headline: "Comfort you don't throw away." Button: "Find your scent." Error: "Hmm, that email doesn't look right — mind checking it?" Sign-off: "Warmly, the Fernloom table."
sections.intro: One line for each surface — your go-to reference when stuck.

fields.label: Rewrite a cold error message the kind way.
Your email sign-off + a social bio line.

sections.title: Call-to-Action Language
sections.tag: How you ask — without sounding like a used-car ad.
sections.desc: A CTA should feel like the next natural step in a conversation, not a command or a countdown. The strongest brands ban false urgency ("Only 3 left!! Ends tonight!!") and write invitations instead. Set your rule once and every button gets easier.
sections.ex: Rule: invite, don't pressure. Yes: "Find your scent," "Come take a look," "Save your spot." No: "BUY NOW," "Don't miss out!," fake countdowns. By channel: softer on social, clearer on the site.
sections.intro: Set a philosophy, then draw the line.

fields.label: Your CTA philosophy in one line.
Three CTAs you'd use — and three you'd never.
A CTA for your site, an email, and a post.

sections.title: Where Your Voice Deploys
sections.tag: Full personality in some places; plain and neutral in others.
sections.desc: Your full brand voice isn't for every context. On your own turf — site, social, packaging — turn it all the way up. In neutral or gatekept places — a wholesale line-sheet, a legal doc, a marketplace listing, a résumé — a stripped, professional voice often wins. Decide by the reader's intent, not habit.
sections.ex: Full voice: website, Instagram, packaging, newsletters. Neutral voice: wholesale line-sheets, retailer portals, legal/returns policy. The rule: "If they came to feel us, full voice. If they came to transact or verify, keep it clean."
sections.intro: Draw your two lists and the rule that sorts them.

fields.label: Where does your FULL voice deploy?
Where do you strip it to neutral-professional?

sections.title: Proposal & Pitch Writing
sections.tag: Prove you get it — without giving away the blueprint. (Skip if you don't pitch or propose.)
sections.desc: If you ever write proposals or pitches, this one rule protects your value: show deep understanding of their world, but hold the exact "how" until you're hired. Over-detailed proposals let a client hand your plan to someone cheaper. Demonstrate competence, then pull one complex piece a real expert would flag and ask a smart question about it.
sections.exWho: A maker pitching a wholesale account
sections.ex: "You're expanding into gifting, and your current candles don't survive shipping to warm climates. We'd redesign the vessel and the pour for heat stability, and rethink the unboxing for gifters. One question first: are your peak orders summer weddings, or holiday? That changes the whole approach." (Names their world, states the approach generally, asks one expert question, opens a conversation — no step-by-step.)
sections.intro: Four moves. Competence without the recipe.

fields.label: Name their world / their real problem in a sentence.
State your approach in general terms only (no step-by-step).
One smart clarifying question a real expert would ask.
A conversational close (not a hard pitch).

sections.title: Writing Under Friction
sections.tag: How you sound when someone's upset — or disagrees.
sections.desc: Anyone can sound good on a launch day. Your brand is really tested in a complaint, a refund, a disagreement. A steady move: don't argue — acknowledge, offer a third option, and lead people to the next step. And decide how care shows up in your words, so hard moments still feel like you.
sections.ex: "You're right, that arrived cracked and that's frustrating — I'd feel the same. Here's what I'd love to do: a fresh one out today, or a refund, your call. And I'll pack this batch with extra padding so it doesn't happen again."
sections.intro: Set your friction move, then practice it.

fields.label: Your rule for disagreement.
fields.hint: e.g., acknowledge → offer a third option → next step. Never argue.

fields.label: How does care show up in your words?
Draft a reply to an unhappy customer.

sections.title: Humor & How You Close
sections.tag: What you joke about, and how you say goodbye.
sections.desc: Humor is personality — but it needs guardrails. Decide what your brand laughs at (usually a warm, observational wink) and what's off-limits (self-deprecation that undercuts you, sarcasm that stings, jokes at anyone's expense). Then decide how you close — the best sign-offs leave people with warmth and a clear next step.
sections.ex: Humor: a gentle wink at "the candle graveyard of half-burned jars." Never: self-deprecation, mean sarcasm. Closes with: a small warmth + a clear next step — "Go light something good. (New scents drop Friday.)"
sections.intro: Two guardrails and a goodbye.

fields.label: What does your humor laugh at?

sections.title: Inclusive & Accessible Language
sections.tag: Writing so everyone can read it, and everyone feels welcome.
sections.desc: Inclusive, accessible language reaches more people and treats them with respect — and it makes your writing clearer for everyone. Three habits carry most of it: plain language, neutral, people-first terms, and alt text on every meaningful image.
sections.ex: Instead of: "Perfect for the busy housewife." We write: "Perfect for anyone whose days move fast." Alt-text habit: every photo gets a plain description.
sections.intro: Three small habits that become second nature.

fields.label: Rewrite one phrase that assumes too much.
Your alt-text habit, in one sentence.

sections.title: Multilingual & Localization
sections.tag: Reaching new languages without losing yourself. (Skip until you go global.)
sections.desc: The day you serve another language, one rule saves you: translate meaning, not words. A literal translation of a slogan usually lands flat or wrong. Localize the feeling, adapt idioms, and where it matters, get a native speaker's eyes on it.
sections.ex: "Light something good" wouldn't translate word-for-word — in each market it becomes the closest phrase that carries warmth + a small daily ritual, checked by a local maker friend.
sections.intro: Set your languages and your translation philosophy.

sections.title: The Voice Test & Pre-Publish Check
sections.tag: One gut-check that keeps everything on-brand.
sections.desc: The fastest quality control is a single question you run every draft through — a "would this kill the vibe if I said it out loud?" test. Pair it with a short NEVER sounds like / ALWAYS sounds like table and a pre-publish checklist, and your voice stays consistent even on your busiest day.
sections.ex: The test: "Would I say this to a customer across the counter?" Never sounds like: a corporate memo, a hype ad, an apology spiral. Always sounds like: a maker who cares. Checklist: On-voice? Clear? Kind? One idea? Typo-free? Right tone for the moment?
sections.intro: Write your test, your table, and your checklist.

fields.label: Three "NEVER sounds like" / three "ALWAYS sounds like."

parts.name: Logo
parts.blurb: Your logo is the face people learn to recognize in a glance. This part gives you room to place it, take it apart, define how it flexes, set the rules that keep it sharp — and, at the end, a brief you can hand straight to a designer.

sections.title: Your Primary Logo
sections.tag: The one people will learn by heart.
sections.desc: Your primary logo is the main, full version you'll use most. Keep the highest-quality files you have (a vector SVG or EPS is best — it scales to any size without blurring). Place it below so it lives in one home you can always find.
sections.ex: A hand-drawn fern frond beside the wordmark in a warm serif — friendly, made-by-hand, unmistakable at a glance.
sections.intro: Drop your primary logo in the box, then note what files you have.

fields.label: File formats I have (SVG / PNG / EPS / PDF)
What my logo means / the story behind it

sections.title: Anatomy & Construction
sections.tag: The parts your logo is made of — named, so you can protect each one.
sections.desc: Every logo is built from parts: the symbol (the picture or mark), the wordmark (your name set in type), and sometimes a tagline lockup. Naming the parts and noting how they're spaced — the proportion between mark and words, the gap between them — means anyone rebuilding your logo gets it right instead of eyeballing it. This is optional, but it's the difference between a logo that stays itself and one that slowly drifts.
sections.ex: Symbol: the frond. Wordmark: "Fernloom Goods" in Fraunces Medium. The gap between frond and word = the width of one leaflet. The frond's height = the cap-height of the word. Lock those two ratios and the logo always looks intentional.
sections.intro: Place your logo, then draw the guides — mark the mark, the wordmark, and the key measurements between them.

fields.label: Place your logo and mark its parts + spacing (the mark, the wordmark, the gap between)
The proportion that must stay fixed

sections.title: Logo Variations
sections.tag: The same logo, dressed for every situation.
sections.desc: One logo is never enough in practice. You'll want a stacked version for tight spaces, a mark/icon for tiny spots like app icons and favicons, a one-color version, and a reversed version for dark backgrounds. Place each below so you always grab the right one.
sections.ex: Full logo for the site header · just the fern mark for the Instagram avatar · a single-ink version for stamps and packaging · a cream version for dark photos.
sections.intro: Place each variation you have. Leave blanks for the ones you still need to make — that's your to-do list.

sections.title: Lockups & Monogram
sections.tag: Fixed arrangements you never rebuild by hand.
sections.desc: A lockup is a set arrangement of your logo elements — inline (mark beside words), stacked (mark above words), and monogram-only (just your initials or mark) — saved as finished files so nobody eyeballs the spacing each time. A monogram is your shorthand: initials or a simplified mark for the smallest spaces, where the full logo would turn to mush. Having these ready is what lets your brand shrink to a favicon or a stamp without falling apart.
sections.ex: Inline lockup for the website header · stacked lockup for packaging labels · an "M+frond" monogram for the app icon, the wax seal, and the social avatar. Three files, chosen by how much room the space gives.
sections.intro: Place each lockup you'll standardize, and design a monogram for the tiniest spots.

sections.title: Clearspace, Size & Fallback
sections.tag: Give it room, never shrink it past legible — and know what to swap in when it's tiny.
sections.desc: Clearspace is the empty margin you always keep around the logo so nothing crowds it (a common rule: the height of one letter). Minimum size is the smallest you'll let it go before it turns to mush. And the piece most brand books skip — a fallback rule: when the space is smaller than your minimum, you don't shrink the full logo, you switch to a simpler version (stacked → mark → monogram). Setting all three keeps your logo readable literally everywhere, from a billboard to a browser tab.
sections.ex: Clearspace = the height of the "M" on all sides. Minimum full logo = 120px wide (screen), 0.75in (print). Below that: drop to the fern mark; below 32px, drop to the monogram. Never squeeze the full logo into a space it can't be read in.
sections.intro: Sketch your clearspace, lock your minimums, then write your fallback ladder.

fields.label: Place your logo and mark the clearspace around it
My fallback ladder (full logo → ___ → ___ → monogram, and at what sizes)

sections.title: Colorways & Backgrounds
sections.tag: Which colors your logo is allowed to wear, and where it can sit.
sections.desc: Decide the exact approved colors your logo may appear in (full-color, all-black, all-white/reversed) and which backgrounds each one is cleared for. If your logo ever sits on a photo, set a rule for keeping it readable — a minimum contrast, or a scrim behind it — and if you use it as a faint watermark, set a lowest opacity it can't go below (a common floor is 70%) so it never disappears into mud. This is what stops a logo from becoming unreadable the moment it leaves your control.
sections.ex: Full-color on cream or white only · all-charcoal on light photos · cream reversed on dark photos or clay. On busy photos: a soft dark scrim behind it. Watermark never below 70% opacity. Never full-color on sage — too little contrast.
sections.intro: Show each approved colorway on the background it's cleared for, and set your floors.

sections.title: Logo Misuse
sections.tag: The "please don't" page — it protects your brand.
sections.desc: Showing what not to do is as important as the logo itself. It stops well-meaning people (and printers, and partners) from stretching, recoloring, or cluttering your logo. Mark up each box with the "don't" it shows — and keep this page handy to send to anyone who'll ever place your logo.
sections.ex: Don't stretch it · don't change the colors · don't rotate it · don't add drop shadows · don't crowd it · don't put it on a busy photo · don't outline it · don't rearrange the parts.
sections.intro: Place a "wrong" version in each box and label the rule it breaks. Add your own at the bottom.

fields.label: My own "never" (something specific to my logo)

sections.title: Your Logo Designer Brief
sections.tag: If you're hiring this out — the one page that gets you the right logo.
sections.desc: If you don't build the logo yourself, this is what you hand a designer. A good brief doesn't tell them what to draw — it tells them who you are, what feeling to hit, what to avoid, and what files you need back. Fill this in and you'll get a logo that fits, on the first or second try, instead of a dozen rounds of "not quite." Skip this section if you already have your logo.
sections.exWho: Fernloom Goods' brief, in one breath
sections.ex: "Warm, hand-made home-goods brand for people who keep things. Feeling: honest, a little ceremonial, never precious. Loves: botanical, warm serifs, single-ink stamps. Avoids: cold minimalism, gradients, trendy. Deliver: vector master + stacked, mark, one-color, reversed; SVG + PNG + PDF."
sections.intro: Answer each — this becomes a brief you can paste into an email or a Bonsai project.

fields.label: Who you are, in one line.
The feeling the logo must give.
fields.hint: Three words is plenty.

fields.label: Styles you love / styles you refuse.
Every file & variation you need back.
fields.hint: Formats + lockups + colorways.

parts.name: Color Palette
parts.blurb: Color is the fastest way people feel your brand. This part gives you space to lay out a full seven-color palette, lock every code right beside it, give each color a job, save your gradients and combinations by season, and prove they're readable.

sections.title: Your Seven-Color Palette
sections.tag: All seven colors — each with its codes locked right underneath it.
sections.desc: Lay out your full palette here: seven colors, each in its own card. Paint the box, name it, then lock the codes lined up right underneath — HEX for screens, RGB for digital, CMYK for print — so the color and its exact numbers always live together. Seven gives you room for a base, a couple of supports, a spark, and a neutral or two. You don't have to fill all seven — leave any you don't need blank.
sections.ex: Clay (warmth) · Cream (calm base) · Sage (grounding) · Charcoal (ink/text) · Ember (the spark) · Terracotta (deep accent) · Oat (soft neutral). Each one carries its HEX, RGB, and CMYK on the same card.
sections.intro: Paint each box, then lock its codes on the lines directly beneath it — color and codes, together.

sections.title: Print & Physical Color
sections.tag: The extra codes your seven colors need to survive off-screen.
sections.desc: Screens glow; ink and thread and paint don't. If your brand ever gets printed, embroidered, or painted, each of your seven colors needs two more things: an HSB value (handy for making lighter/darker tints) and a physical match — a Pantone or RAL number a printer or manufacturer can hit exactly. One honest caveat worth writing down: the CMYK on your screen is only a guess, so always ask for a printed proof before a big run. This whole page is optional — skip it if you're digital-only.
sections.ex: HSB 30/84/71 · Pantone 1535 C (nearest). On uncoated stock it reads a touch browner, so Fernloom always proofs the labels first. The other six colors each get the same treatment.
sections.intro: One row per color — the same seven from your palette. Only if you print or make physical goods.

fields.label: Write in each box: HSB · Pantone/RAL (nearest)

sections.title: Functional Color Roles
sections.tag: The colors that do a job — buttons, alerts, links.
sections.desc: Beyond "which colors are pretty together," some colors have a function, especially on a website or app. You need one for the main action (buttons, links), and usually a success (green-ish "it worked"), a warning (amber "heads up"), and an error (red "something's wrong"). Assigning these once means every button and every alert across everything you build looks like it belongs to you — not the default blue every template ships with. Pull these from your seven colors wherever you can. Skip this if you're print-only or personal.
sections.ex: Action / buttons: Ember · Links: Clay · Success: Sage · Warning: a soft amber · Error: a warm brick red · Neutral text: Charcoal. Now every form and button on the site feels hand-made, not stock.
sections.intro: Assign a color to each job. Reuse your seven colors — that's encouraged.

sections.title: Color Hierarchy & 60/30/10
sections.tag: Which color leads, which supports, which sparks.
sections.desc: Seven colors is a wardrobe, not an outfit — you don't wear them all at once. The 60/30/10 rule keeps any single layout balanced: ~60% a base color, ~30% a support, ~10% an accent. Fill the bar below to see the balance at a glance. This one ratio is why some brands feel calm and others feel loud — it's the single most useful color habit you can keep.
sections.ex: 60% Cream (base) · 30% Clay + Sage (support) · 10% Ember (spark). The other three colors wait in the wings for accents and special pieces.
sections.intro: Color in the bar, then name which of your seven plays each role.

sections.title: Schemes & Gradients
sections.tag: Three ready combinations and three gradients, so you never mix from scratch.
sections.desc: Save three locked color schemes — trios from your seven that always work together — and three gradients (one color flowing into another). Having these saved means when you sit down to make a post or a slide, you reach for a combination that's already right instead of guessing. Note what each one is for, so you pick by mood, not by chance.
sections.ex: Schemes: "Warm Shelf" (Clay + Cream + Ember, for product shots) · "Quiet" (Sage + Cream + Charcoal, for journal posts) · "Rich" (Terracotta + Oat + Charcoal, for the holidays). Gradients: Ember→Clay (newsletter header) · Sage→Cream (soft backgrounds) · Terracotta→Charcoal (covers).
sections.intro: Fill three scheme strips and three gradient strips, and name what each is for.

fields.label: Scheme 1 — three colors — what it's for
Scheme 2 — three colors — what it's for
Scheme 3 — three colors — what it's for
Gradient 1 — color → color — where it's used
Gradient 2 — color → color — where it's used
Gradient 3 — color → color — where it's used

sections.title: Seasonal Palettes
sections.tag: A palette for each season — still unmistakably you.
sections.desc: A palette for every season lets your brand feel fresh through the year without ever feeling like a different company — because each one is built from your same seven colors, just re-weighted. A warmer, cozier mix for autumn; something lighter and airier for spring. Build one for each of the four seasons below. Optional — skip any (or all) if you'd rather keep one fixed palette year-round.
sections.ex: Spring: Cream + Sage + pale Ember (airy). Summer: Ember + Oat + Clay (bright, warm). Autumn: Terracotta + deep Ember + Charcoal (cozy). Winter: Charcoal + Cream + Sage (quiet, crisp). All seven colors, just re-weighted.
sections.intro: Build a palette for each season from your seven colors — one placeholder per season.

sections.title: Combinations & Contrast
sections.tag: Approved pairings that are always easy to read.
sections.desc: Not every color looks good — or reads well — on every other color. Lock a few approved pairings (text color on background color) from your seven, and check each for contrast. There's an actual standard: for normal text, aim for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (any free "contrast checker" online gives you the number). If it fails, it's not accessible, no matter how pretty — and some of your readers literally can't read it. Fill each box with a real pairing and a test word.
sections.ex: Charcoal on Cream = 12:1 ✓ · Cream on Clay = 5.2:1 ✓ · Clay on Cream = 3.1:1 ✗ (fails for body text — large headings only) · never Sage on Cream (2:1, too faint).
sections.intro: Fill each box with a pairing, write a test word, and note the contrast ratio (aim 4.5:1+).

Pairing 2 — write a word — ratio ___ : 1 · pass? ✓/✗
