parts.name: Typography
parts.blurb: Type is your voice made visible. This part gives you room to place your fonts, show them at every size, set the hierarchy that makes anything you make instantly readable — and lock the small technical rules (minimum sizes, spacing, licensing) that keep it clean everywhere.

sections.title: Your Typefaces
sections.tag: A small crew of fonts, each with a job.
sections.desc: Pick a display font for headlines, a body font for everything you read, and (optionally) an accent font for flourishes. Keep it to two or three — more than that and things start to feel messy. Place a specimen of each below and note where to get it, so you or anyone helping you always uses the real thing.
sections.ex: Display: Fraunces (warm serif) · Body: Inter (clean sans) · Accent: Caveat (handwritten), used rarely.
sections.intro: Place a specimen of each font and note its details.

sections.title: Weights & Styles You'll Use
sections.tag: Which cuts of each font are in — and which are off-limits.
sections.desc: Most fonts come in many weights — thin, light, regular, medium, bold, black — plus italics. You don't use them all. Decide the specific weights you'll actually use for each font, so your work stays consistent instead of grabbing a random "semibold" one day and "black" the next. A good habit: pick one weight for headings, one for body, one for emphasis, and retire the rest. Note any letter-spacing (tracking) a font needs — some display fonts and all-caps need a little air to breathe.
sections.ex: Fraunces: Medium for H1–H2, that's it. Inter: Regular for body, Semibold for emphasis and buttons, nothing heavier. All-caps labels get +8% tracking. Italics only in Fraunces, for pull-quotes.
sections.intro: Lock the weights that are in. Everything you don't list is off-limits — that's the point.

sections.title: Your Type Scale
sections.tag: The same fonts, sized and styled for every job on the page.
sections.desc: A type scale is your set of sizes — from big headline down to tiny caption — so text always has a clear order. Write each level in its box at the size you'd really use, and lock the font, weight, and size beside it. Note both print points and screen pixels if you work in both. This becomes your go-to reference forever.
sections.ex: H1 Fraunces Medium 40pt / 54px · H2 Fraunces 28 / 36px · H3 Fraunces 20 / 26px · Body Inter Regular 16 / 16px · Caption Inter 12 / 13px.
sections.intro: Write each level at its real size in the box, and lock the details.

sections.title: Spacing, Line Length & Legibility Floors
sections.tag: The invisible rules that make text easy — or exhausting — to read.
sections.desc: Three quiet settings do most of the work of readable text. Line spacing (leading) — body text usually breathes best at about 1.5× its size. Line length (measure) — aim for 50–75 characters per line; longer and the eye gets lost coming back. And legibility floors — the smallest size each font stays readable, below which you switch to a simpler one. Setting these once means everything you write is comfortable to read without you thinking about it again.
sections.ex: Body leading 1.6 · line length capped ~68 characters · Inter never below 12px, Fraunces headings never below 18px (below that, drop the serif and set it in Inter). Never set long paragraphs in the accent font.
sections.intro: Lock your comfort settings.

fields.label: Smallest readable size per font (and what you drop to below it)

sections.title: Pairing & Hierarchy
sections.tag: How your fonts work together on a real page.
sections.desc: Hierarchy is how the eye knows what to read first. A headline in your display font, a subhead, then body in your reading font — that contrast guides people through. Mock up a real block below to see your fonts in action together. One rule of thumb: two font families per layout is plenty; a third only as a rare accent.
sections.ex: Big Fraunces headline → small-caps Inter subhead → easy Inter body. Lots of breathing room between them.
sections.intro: Lay out a sample headline + subhead + paragraph using your fonts.

fields.label: Mock up a headline, a subhead, and a paragraph here
One rule for your hierarchy (e.g., "always leave space above headings")

sections.title: Font Files, Licensing & Fallbacks
sections.tag: The boring page that saves you a legal headache and a broken website.
sections.desc: Two practical things brand books forget. First, licensing: know whether each font is free for commercial use, or needs a license for web/print/apps — using a font you don't have rights to is a real risk once you're making money. Second, a fallback stack: if your font fails to load on a website or isn't installed on someone's computer, what shows instead? Naming a close web-safe backup (and where your font files live) keeps your brand from silently breaking. Skip the web parts if you're print-only.
sections.ex: Fraunces & Inter — both free, open-source, commercial OK (from Google Fonts). Files stored in the brand drive + on the site. Web fallback: Fraunces → Georgia, serif; Inter → Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif. Caveat: the accent font is desktop-license only — never embed it on the site.
sections.intro: Note the rights and the backups — future-you will be grateful.

parts.name: Visuals
parts.blurb: Photos, icons, patterns, effects, and layout are the atmosphere around your words. This part gives you space to build a whole look — a moodboard, a way of directing images, an icon system, textures, signature effects, and the way it all sits on a page.

sections.title: Imagery & Photography
sections.tag: The kind of pictures that feel like you.
sections.desc: Your imagery style is a promise: warm and natural, or bold and graphic, or clean and minimal. Build a little moodboard below — six images that feel right together — then name the style in words so it's repeatable.
sections.ex: Natural light, warm tones, real hands at work, lots of negative space. Never harsh flash or staged stock photos.
sections.intro: Fill your moodboard, then put the style into words.

sections.title: Art Direction
sections.tag: Not just what a photo looks like — how to actually make one.
sections.desc: A moodboard shows the destination; art direction is the directions to get there. It's the difference between "warm photos" and a repeatable recipe: the lighting (soft daylight? warm lamp glow?), the subjects (hands, faces, product alone?), the styling (what's in frame, what people wear, the props), and the composition (close and intimate, or wide with lots of air). Write it down and anyone — you, a photographer, an AI image tool — can make an image that already belongs to your brand. Include a short do / don't, because ruling things out is half the job. If you also use illustration, note its build recipe too.
sections.ex: Lighting: soft window light, late afternoon, warm. Subjects: hands mid-work, product in a lived-in home. Styling: linen, raw wood, one imperfect thing in frame. Composition: close, off-center, room to breathe. Do: real texture, honest mess. Don't: flash, cold white, staged perfection, cosplay props. Illustration: warm line drawings over a soft color wash, a little grain on top.
sections.intro: Write your recipe so any image can be made to match.

fields.label: Subjects / who or what's in frame

sections.title: Icons & Graphics
sections.tag: The small visual language that ties things together.
sections.desc: Icons and simple graphics should share one style — same weight, same corners, same feel — so they look like a family. Beyond the look, a few build rules keep them consistent as your set grows: the stroke weight (line thickness), whether corners are rounded or sharp, the grid they're drawn on (a simple square keeps them the same visual size), and the file formats you keep them in (SVG for anything digital). Place samples below and lock the rules.
sections.ex: Thin single-line icons, 2px stroke, rounded corners, hand-drawn feel, all drawn inside a 24px square so they sit evenly in a row. Kept as SVG + PNG. Never chunky, never 3-D, never mixed with someone else's icon pack.
sections.intro: Place icon samples and set the build rules that keep the set consistent.

sections.title: Patterns & Textures
sections.tag: The extras that make things feel finished.
sections.desc: A signature pattern or texture — a paper grain, a repeating motif, a subtle background — adds richness and makes empty space feel intentional. To keep it usable, note a few things per pattern: the scale (how big it tiles), the opacity (how faint it sits behind text so it never fights the words), and where it's allowed (packaging only? backgrounds only?). A pattern with no rules quickly becomes clutter. Place any you use below — optional, but a lovely touch.
sections.ex: Clay paper-grain texture — full-bleed on packaging, ~8% opacity behind headings, never behind body text. Tiny fern motif — tiles at ~1 inch, used on wrapping and section dividers only, never on the website body.
sections.intro: Place your patterns, and note the scale, opacity, and where each is allowed.

sections.title: Effects & Filters
sections.tag: The finishing touches you put on top — used sparingly, always the same way.
sections.desc: Effects are the treatments you apply over photos and graphics: a signature photo filter (a consistent color grade so every image feels like one set), a duotone or color wash, a soft grain or glow, a specific shadow style. The danger with effects is overuse — so the rule is to pick one or two, define them precisely (which colors, how strong), and apply them the same way every time. Done right, a filter is the fastest way to make a pile of mismatched photos suddenly look like yours. Fully optional — skip if your brand is clean and effect-free.
sections.ex: Signature grade: warm up shadows, lift highlights slightly, pull greens toward sage — applied to every product photo. Grain: very light, film-like, on hero images only. Shadows: soft and warm, never hard black. That's the whole kit — nothing else gets added.
sections.intro: Define one or two signature effects — precisely enough to repeat. Leave blank if you use none.

fields.label: The recipe (which colors / how strong) so it's repeatable
The limit — where these effects are NOT used

sections.title: Layout & Composition
sections.tag: How everything sits together on a page.
sections.desc: Layout is the quiet skill that makes everything look professional: consistent margins, a sense of alignment, and generous space. You don't need to be a designer — just a few rules keep every page feeling like the same brand. Sketch a sample layout and jot your spacing rules.
sections.ex: Wide margins, everything aligned to a simple grid, one clear focal point per page, and never crowd the edges.
sections.intro: Give yourself room here — sketch two go-to layouts, then set your spacing rules. The more space you take to work this out, the more consistent everything you make will be.

fields.label: Sketch your main layout — grid, margins, columns, where the logo / headline / image / body go
An alternate layout (e.g. a wide / hero version)
Another layout (e.g. a content / text-heavy page)
Alignment / grid rule (how many columns, what lines up)
One focal-point rule (what the eye should hit first)

parts.name: Motion & Animation
parts.blurb: The moment your brand moves — a logo that assembles, a button that responds, a page that eases in — it stops being a picture and starts feeling alive. This part is fully optional, but if your brand lives on screens, motion is where it earns personality. Skip it entirely if you're print-only.

sections.title: Your Motion Principles
sections.tag: A few rules that make every animation feel like the same hand.
sections.desc: Before any specific animation, set the feel. Good motion is alive but intentional — it guides the eye, it never shows off. Decide your brand's tempo (calm and slow? snappy and quick?) and its character (gentle eases, or crisp mechanical moves). And one rule that matters more than people realize: respect reduced motion — some people get dizzy or sick from movement, and every phone and browser has a "reduce motion" setting. Honoring it (calmer or no animation for those users) isn't optional politeness; it's basic accessibility.
sections.ex: Motion is slow, warm, and organic — things ease in like a curtain settling, never bounce or snap. Tempo: unhurried (0.4–0.6s). Nothing moves just for decoration. And when a visitor has "reduce motion" on, everything simply fades gently instead of sliding.
sections.intro: Set the feel of your motion in a few honest words.

fields.label: Our reduced-motion promise (what happens for people who opt out of movement)

sections.title: Your Motion Vocabulary
sections.tag: The specific movements that are unmistakably yours.
sections.desc: Just like you have signature words, you can have signature movements — the handful you reuse everywhere so the brand feels coherent. Think about how things enter (fade up? slide in?), how they respond when touched (a gentle grow? a color shift?), and how the screen transitions between pages. Naming three or four moves means whoever builds your site or edits your video reaches for your motion, not a random template's.
sections.ex: Enter: content fades up 12px as you scroll to it. Respond: buttons warm from clay to ember on hover, no movement. Transition: pages cross-fade over 0.5s. Signature: the frond in the logo slowly unfurls on the homepage. Four moves, used everywhere.
sections.intro: Name your handful of signature moves — describe each in plain words.

fields.label: One signature move that's just yours

sections.title: Logo Animation
sections.tag: The little film your logo plays when it arrives.
sections.desc: An animated logo is the flourish for video intros, loading screens, and social stings. It doesn't need to be fancy — it needs to be yours and short (2–5 seconds is plenty). Storyboard it in a few beats: how it starts, how it builds, how it settles. Writing the beats and rough timing down means you can hand it to any motion designer, or rebuild it yourself, and get the same result. Optional — skip if you don't do video or intros.
sections.ex: 0–1s: the wordmark fades up, letter by letter. 1–2s: the frond draws itself in beside it, like ink settling. 2–3s: one frond gently unfurls, then it holds. Warm, unhurried, done.
sections.intro: Storyboard your logo animation in three or four beats, with rough timing.

fields.label: The feeling it should leave (in one line)

sections.title: Micro-Interactions
sections.tag: The tiny responses that make a screen feel considerate.
sections.desc: Micro-interactions are the small acknowledgements a screen gives back: a button that dips when clicked, a form field that glows when you tap it, a little check when something saves, a gentle loading state. They're small, but they're the difference between an interface that feels cheap and one that feels cared-for. Decide how yours behave — consistently — and the whole product feels intentional. Optional; most relevant for websites and apps.
sections.ex: Buttons: warm one shade + dip 1px on click. Fields: a soft sage glow on focus. Success: a small ember check that fades in. Loading: three dots breathing slowly, never a harsh spinner. Small, warm, consistent.
sections.intro: Decide how your small moments respond. Reuse these everywhere.

parts.name: Characters & Mascots
parts.blurb: Some brands have a face that isn't the logo — a mascot, a spokes-character, an avatar, a recurring illustrated figure. Done well, a character carries feeling and story no logo can. This part is fully optional; many brands never need one. But if yours has a character (or could), this is where it comes to life.

sections.title: Do You Even Need One?
sections.tag: A character is a commitment — decide honestly before you build one.
sections.desc: A character is different from your logo and different from your voice. A logo marks; a character acts — it can wave, react, guide, and show up in stories. That's powerful, but it's also work to keep consistent. So first, the honest question: does your brand actually benefit from a face? Mascots shine for brands that teach, entertain, speak to kids or communities, or want warmth and memorability. They're overkill for a serious B2B consultancy or a minimalist product. There's no wrong answer — including "not for us."
sections.ex: Decided yes, lightly: a little illustrated bee named "Buzz" who appears in the newsletter and on packaging inserts — never as the logo, just as a friendly guide. Warmth without turning the whole brand into a cartoon.
sections.intro: Answer honestly. "No" is a complete and valid answer — skip the rest of this part if so.

fields.label: Would a character actually help my brand? Why or why not?
If yes — what job would it do? (guide, teach, mascot, avatar, story)

sections.title: Character Profile
sections.tag: Give it a name, a personality, and a reason to exist.
sections.desc: A character that isn't defined drifts — different every time someone draws or writes it. Pin it down like a person: a name, a one-line essence (who they are), a personality (how they act), and their role in your world (what they're for). This is what keeps a mascot recognizably itself whether it's on a sticker, in a video, or answering a chat. If you have more than one character, do a profile for each — and note how they relate.
sections.ex: Name: Buzz. Essence: a small, earnest bee who believes everything handmade is worth the wait. Personality: warm, curious, a little clumsy, never sarcastic. Role: the friendly guide who introduces new products and thanks customers. Never used to sell hard — only to welcome.
sections.intro: Build your character like you'd introduce a friend.

sections.title: Look & Expressions
sections.tag: The visual model — and the range of feelings it can show.
sections.desc: Now make it drawable. Place a model sheet — your character from a couple of angles, plus a few expressions (happy, thinking, celebrating) and maybe a pose or two. The expressions matter more than people expect: a character's power is that it can react, so having a small set of ready faces means it can show up appropriately in a launch, an apology, or a thank-you. Lock the non-negotiables (proportions, colors) so it stays on-model everywhere.
sections.ex: Round body, two tiny wings, always in the brand's ember and charcoal. Four faces: delighted, curious, grateful, sleepy. One rule: the wings are always soft, never sharp — and Buzz is never bigger than the logo.
sections.intro: Place your model sheet and a small set of expressions.

sections.title: Where It Shows Up (& Where It Doesn't)
sections.tag: A character with no boundaries becomes noise.
sections.desc: The final discipline: decide where your character appears and, just as important, where it doesn't. Used everywhere, a mascot gets tiring and starts to undercut you in serious moments. Used with intention — the right places, the right moments — it becomes something people look forward to. Map its home turf and its no-go zones so it always lands as a delight, never a distraction.
sections.ex: Appears: newsletter header, packaging thank-you insert, 404 page, kids' gift line. Never: the main logo lockup, invoices, wholesale/pitch documents, or anything about a shipping problem — serious moments stay Buzz-free.
sections.intro: Map the home turf and the no-go zones.

parts.name: Collateral & Applications
parts.blurb: This is where your brand leaves the workbook and shows up in the real world — on cards, decks, posts, packaging, and in the feeling people carry away. Place your key pieces here, with the exact specs that keep everything looking like it came from the same place.

sections.title: Stationery & Business Cards
sections.tag: The small printed pieces that make you feel official.
sections.desc: Business cards, letterhead, and email signatures are tiny brand ambassadors. Keep them simple, consistent, and unmistakably yours. Place your designs (or your plan for them) below.
sections.ex: Cream card, clay logo, one line of contact in Inter. Email signature: name, title, a single fern mark.
sections.intro: Place each piece, or sketch what it should look like.

sections.title: Marketing Collateral
sections.tag: Flyers, brochures, one-pagers, and decks.
sections.desc: Anything you hand out or send to explain yourself — a flyer, a brochure, a pitch deck, a one-pager. Set a simple template so these always feel on-brand instead of made from scratch each time. A tip that saves hours: note the font and color recipe per piece (which font for the headline, which color for the accent) right on the template, so filling it in is paint-by-numbers.
sections.ex: Flyer recipe: big photo up top, Fraunces headline in clay, three product highlights in Inter, one ember call-to-action button. Deck recipe: cream slides, Fraunces titles, one idea per slide.
sections.intro: Place your go-to templates, and note the recipe on each.

fields.label: Presentation / deck slide — font + color recipe

sections.title: Social Media Templates
sections.tag: Posts and stories that are instantly recognizable — at the right size.
sections.desc: People scroll fast. A consistent post style — same fonts, colors, and layout — makes them stop because they recognize you. Two things make this effortless: reusable templates, and building them at the correct pixel sizes so nothing gets awkwardly cropped. The common ones: feed post 1080×1080, portrait 1080×1350, story/reel 1080×1920, and link-preview/OG image 1200×630. Build once at these sizes and posting stays quick and sharp.
sections.ex: Square posts (1080²) with a photo and a small clay caption bar; stories (1080×1920) with a cream background and one line of Fraunces; a 1200×630 link image for blog shares. Same three colors, one watermark, every time.
sections.intro: Place your templates at the right sizes (noted under each).

fields.label: My fixed post rules (watermark, max colors, which font)

sections.title: Merchandise & Packaging
sections.tag: Where your brand becomes something people hold.
sections.desc: Packaging, labels, stickers, apparel — the tangible touchpoints. Even if you're digital, a branded thank-you or a shipping detail can turn a customer into a fan. If you make physical goods, note the production method per item (printed vs. embroidered vs. foil-stamped vs. engraved) — because your logo has to be prepared differently for each, and a design that looks great on screen can fall apart in thread or foil. Place any you use (optional).
sections.ex: Kraft box (flexo print), clay tissue, a hand-stamped thank-you card, a foil-stamped logo on the candle lid, and an embroidered apron (simplified to the fern mark — the full wordmark is too fine to stitch).
sections.intro: Place your packaging/merch, and note how each is produced.

sections.title: The Brand Experience
sections.tag: Your brand isn't just seen — it's felt , at every step.
sections.desc: The deepest layer of a brand isn't a logo or a color — it's how someone feels moving through it, from the first glimpse to long after they've bought. Map the journey — discovery, first contact, buying/working together, receiving, and after — and name the one feeling you want at each stop. This is what turns a nice-looking brand into one people are loyal to. It also quietly tells you where to put your effort: the steps where the feeling you want and the feeling they'd actually get don't match yet.
sections.ex: Discovery: curious. First contact (site/DM): welcomed, unhurried. Buying: reassured, no pressure. Unboxing: delighted — "this was made for me." After: remembered (a handwritten note, a re-order nudge that feels like a friend, not a funnel).
sections.intro: Walk your person's path and name the feeling you want at each stop.

fields.label: Discovery — the first time they notice you.
fields.hint: One feeling.

fields.label: First contact — site, DM, or conversation.
Receiving — the product, the delivery, the first use.
After — what keeps them coming back.

parts.name: Digital Presence
parts.blurb: Your website, social profiles, and emails are where most people meet you today. This part locks how your brand looks and behaves online, so every screen feels like the same brand.

sections.title: Your Website
sections.tag: Your home base — the one address you own.
sections.desc: Your site is the one place you fully control. Note the colors, fonts, and building blocks (buttons, headers, cards) it uses, and mock the homepage feel below, so a designer or a website builder can match your brand exactly.
sections.ex: Cream background, clay buttons, Fraunces headlines, big product photos, lots of white space. Feels calm and easy to shop.
sections.intro: Mock your homepage, then note the building blocks.

sections.title: Social Profiles
sections.tag: Consistent from platform to platform.
sections.desc: Your profile photo, cover images, and bio should match across every platform so people know they've found the real you. Place your profile assets and lock your handles and bio.
sections.ex: Fern-mark avatar everywhere, same one-line bio: "Small-batch candles in ceramics worth keeping. 🕯️"
sections.intro: Place your profile assets and lock the details.

sections.title: Email
sections.tag: The inbox is personal — show up right.
sections.desc: Your newsletter header, layout, and sign-off carry your brand into a private space. Keep them warm and consistent. Place your email template and note your standard sign-off.
sections.ex: Simple cream header with the logo, one photo, short warm copy, one button. Sign-off: "Warmly, the Fernloom table."
sections.intro: Place your email header/template and lock your sign-off.

parts.name: Print Materials
parts.blurb: Print is forever — you can't edit it once it's out. This short part sets the specs that keep printed pieces crisp, correctly colored, and consistent.

sections.title: Print Standards
sections.tag: The specs that keep print looking sharp.
sections.desc: Print has its own rules. A few settings prevent blurry logos and colors that come out wrong: use 300 DPI images, CMYK color (not screen RGB), and add bleed (extra margin that gets trimmed) so nothing important sits at the very edge. Lock your standards below.
sections.ex: 300 DPI, CMYK, 0.125" bleed, uncoated recycled stock, matte finish.
sections.intro: Lock your print settings once, use them forever.

fields.label: Which colors shift in print? (note any adjustments)

sections.title: Printed Pieces
sections.tag: Your library of physical materials.
sections.desc: Keep a visual record of your printed pieces so reprints and new items stay consistent. Place what you have below.
sections.intro: Place your printed materials (skip any you don't have yet).

parts.name: Environmental Branding
parts.blurb: If your brand ever lives in a physical space — a shop, a studio, a booth, an event — this is how it shows up there. Optional if you're fully digital, but lovely to plan for.

sections.title: Signage & Space
sections.tag: Your brand, standing in the room.
sections.desc: Signs, window decals, wall graphics, and the feel of a space all carry your brand. Even a small studio corner can be on-brand. Place any signage or space designs below.
sections.ex: A hand-painted wooden sign, cream walls, shelves of ceramics, and one big fern mural at the back.
sections.intro: Place signage or a space mood (optional).

sections.title: Events & Booths
sections.tag: Showing up in person, on-brand.
sections.desc: Markets, pop-ups, and events are a chance to be fully yourself in 3-D — table setup, banners, giveaways. Plan the look here (optional).
sections.intro: Place your event / booth setup (optional).

parts.name: Governance & Evolution
parts.blurb: A brand is a living thing — and a valuable one. This part is how you actually roll it out, keep it whole day to day, decide who's allowed to change it, and let it grow on purpose instead of drifting. This is the "be ready" layer: the difference between a brand book you made once and a brand you run.

sections.title: Your Asset Inventory
sections.tag: An honest list of what's built, what isn't, and where it all lives.
sections.desc: The most useful page in any brand system is also the least glamorous: a plain, honest ledger of what actually exists. What's locked and done, what's still to build, and — critically — where the files live so you can find them at 11pm before a deadline. A mature brand names its gaps out loud instead of pretending everything's finished. This one page saves you from "I know I made that logo variation somewhere…"
sections.ex: Done: logo + 4 variations, palette, fonts, voice, post templates (in the brand drive). Not yet: the animated logo, a proper packaging label, an icon set. Files live: master vectors in the brand drive, working files in Affinity, fonts backed up in two places.
sections.intro: List it honestly. The "not yet" column is a feature — it becomes your roadmap.

fields.label: Where all my master files live (and their backup)

sections.title: Your Build Roadmap
sections.tag: The order you'll finish what's not built yet.
sections.desc: Take the "still to build" list and put it in order. Not everything matters equally right now — so sequence by what actually moves you forward. A good rule: prioritize what unblocks money or momentum (the pieces you need to sell, launch, or ship) over pure polish. Naming the order keeps you from the trap of endlessly perfecting one thing while three needed things wait. Rough phases beat a perfect plan.
sections.ex: Phase 1 (now): packaging label + product-photo template — needed to ship the new line. Phase 2: icon set + email template. Phase 3 (nice-to-have): the animated logo. Revenue first, polish last.
sections.intro: Put your unbuilt pieces in phases. Ask of each: does this help me sell/launch, or is it polish?

sections.title: Rollout & Where the Full Brand Applies
sections.tag: Not every surface gets the full brand — decide which do.
sections.desc: Two decisions here. First, rollout order: when you update your brand, do the surfaces people see most first (usually your site and anything client-facing), then social, then the long tail. Second — a subtle but important one — decide where your full branded voice and look apply, and where a plainer, more neutral version is smarter. Your own website, your emails, your content: full brand. But some places (a marketplace profile, a formal document, a platform with its own rules) often call for a more professional-generic register. Drawing that line on purpose keeps your brand from feeling out of place — and keeps you from watering it down where it should be strong.
sections.ex: Rollout: website first, then Instagram, then packaging, then the market booth. Full brand voice & look: own site, newsletter, IG, packaging. Neutral/professional: the wholesale line-sheet and the marketplace listing — buyers there want specs, not story. The two never blur.
sections.intro: Set the order, then draw the line between full-brand and neutral surfaces.

sections.title: Governance & Change Control
sections.tag: Who decides, how things change, and what's not allowed to ship.
sections.desc: This is what keeps a brand from slowly falling apart. Three small commitments. Who decides — name the person (probably you) who has the final say on brand choices, so it doesn't happen by accident. How a locked thing changes — "locked" doesn't mean never, it means changing it is a deliberate act: you write down the reason, fully define the replacement, and re-date the book. And the ship gates — a short list of things that mean "this is not on-brand, don't send it" (wrong logo, off colors, unreadable text). When you have a team or hire help, this page is what you point to.
sections.ex: Decider: the founder, full stop. To change a locked element: write why, design the full replacement, update this book with a new date — no half-changes. Don't-ship gates: logo stretched or recolored · more than three colors on one thing · text that fails contrast · the mascot on a serious document.
sections.intro: Lock your decision rules and your don't-ship list.

sections.title: Staying Consistent
sections.tag: The everyday habits that keep your brand whole.
sections.desc: Consistency is what turns a look into a brand. It's less about rules and more about habits — checking the same handful of things before anything goes out. Tick the habits you'll keep.
sections.intro: Check the ones you'll commit to — add your own.

sections.title: Reviewing & Refreshing
sections.tag: Change on purpose, not by accident.
sections.desc: Brands should evolve — but deliberately. Set a rhythm to revisit this book, decide what still fits, and log what you change so you always know the current version. A little refresh keeps you current; a random one causes drift. Tie this to your governance rule: every change gets a date.
sections.ex: Reviews the brand every 6 months, plus any time it launches something big. Last refresh: softened the logo and added a third scent line. Everything logged and dated.
sections.intro: Set your rhythm, then keep a simple change log.

fields.label: How often will you review your brand?

sections.title: Measuring Brand Health
sections.tag: How to tell if it's working — without chasing vanity numbers.
sections.desc: You don't need a dashboard to know if your brand is healthy — you need the right few signals. Recognition: does your stuff look like you even before the logo shows up? Consistency: when you look across everything, does it feel like one brand? Resonance: do people describe you the way you meant to be felt? Speed: is on-brand work getting faster because your system is doing the heavy lifting? And a quiet caution — don't chase vanity metrics (follower counts, likes) as proof of brand health; they measure reach, not whether the brand is landing. Below is a pulse-check you can run any time.
sections.ex: Healthy signals: a customer reposted a photo and it looked like Fernloom without the logo · three strangers used the word "calm" unprompted · making a new post now takes ten minutes, not an hour. Ignored: the follower number.
sections.intro: Run through these any time. Anything you can't check is your next project.

fields.label: Does my stuff look like me even without the logo?
Across everything, does it feel like one brand?
Do people describe me the way I meant to be felt?
Is on-brand work getting faster to make?
Does my brand still match what I actually do today?
Am I proud to show it?

parts.name: Legal Considerations
parts.blurb: The unglamorous part that protects everything you've built. This is a plain-language starting point — not legal advice — to help you know what to look into and keep track of.

sections.title: Protecting Your Brand
sections.tag: The basics of owning what's yours.
sections.desc: A few things quietly protect your brand: registering your name, considering a trademark for your name and logo, and making sure you actually have the rights to your fonts and images (many need a license for commercial use). You don't have to do it all at once — just know what exists so nothing bites you later.
sections.ex: Registered the business name, filed a trademark for the wordmark, bought commercial licenses for its fonts, and only uses photos it owns or licensed.
sections.intro: Note where you stand — gaps become your to-do list.

fields.label: Font licenses — do you have commercial rights?
Image licenses — do you own or license your photos?

sections.title: Usage & Permissions
sections.tag: Who can use your brand, and how.
sections.desc: As you grow, others will handle your brand — partners, press, collaborators, contractors. A simple usage note (who can use your logo, where, and how) prevents your brand from being used in ways you wouldn't choose.
sections.ex: "Press and stockists may use our logo as-is, on a clean background, with clearspace. No recoloring or altering. Ask us for the files."
sections.intro: Write your simple usage rules.

sections.title: Your Legal Checklist
sections.tag: Everything in one place, tracked.
sections.desc: A running checklist so nothing slips. Tick what's done; the blanks are your next steps.
sections.intro: Check what's handled.

parts.name: Brand Management
parts.blurb: The final part: how you run your brand out in the world, day after day. Simple guidelines for advertising, social, content, and partnerships — so your brand stays strong as you grow.

sections.title: Advertising & Marketing
sections.tag: Show up boldly — and still like yourself.
sections.desc: Ads and campaigns push your brand out to new people. A few guidelines keep them on-brand: your look, your voice, and the promise you always make. Set the guardrails so any ad still feels like you.
sections.ex: "Every ad leads with a real photo and a warm line. No hype, no fake urgency. Always one clear, kind call to action."
sections.intro: Set your advertising guardrails.

sections.title: Social Media Guidelines
sections.tag: How you behave in the feed.
sections.desc: Social is where your brand is most human. Set simple guidelines: what you post about, how you sound, how fast you reply, and how you handle the tough stuff. Consistency here builds real community.
sections.ex: Posts: behind-the-scenes, new scents, slow-living tips. Replies within a day, always warm. Never argues publicly — takes it to DMs.
sections.intro: Set your social rhythm.

fields.label: What we post about (our content pillars)

sections.title: Content & Email Guidelines
sections.tag: Keeping your ongoing content on-brand.
sections.desc: Blogs, newsletters, and regular content are a long game — consistency is what pays off. Set how often you publish, what value you give, and the one thing every piece should do. (Your voice rules live back in Part 3.)
sections.ex: One newsletter a month: a story, a product, a slow-living tip. Every piece teaches or delights before it sells.
sections.intro: Set your content commitments.

sections.title: PR & Partnerships
sections.tag: Choosing who you stand beside.
sections.desc: Press, collaborations, and partners borrow your brand — and lend you theirs. A quick filter for who fits keeps your reputation intact. Decide what a good partner looks like before the offers come.
sections.ex: "We partner with makers who share our values — slow, honest, sustainable. We say no to fast-fashion and anything throwaway."
sections.intro: Set your partnership filter.

fields.label: A good partner for us is…
How we want to be described in press (boilerplate)
